On 1 October 2012 18:31, Kylan Chang <thek...@gmail.com> wrote:
> The model is successfully builded and work well.
> But I like to extract the whole sperical harmonic expansion after fitting
> the model.

That information is accessible from the "result" output, but is a bit
tricky to keep track of.  For this reason, there is a function
"inla.spde.result" that extracts the relevant bits.  It's one of the
as yet undocumented functions...

In your case, the syntax is as follows, where I've assumed that the
spde part of your model formula was called "field":

spde.result = inla.spde.result(result, "field", spde=spde, do.transform=FALSE)

This tells the function to extract the bits of "result" related to the
"field" part of the model, and that the model object is the given spde
model object.  The "do.transform" parameter indicates whether to
transform the log(tau) and log(kappa) parameters (and some other
output) into the external tau and kappa scale.  For non-stationary
models, this can be time-consuming (mostly due to inefficiencies in
the R language) but you can try turning it on with do.transform=TRUE.
Do
  names(spde.result)
on the result for a full listing of the types of output generated; the
names are hopefully fairly self-explanatory.

> By
> "result$joint.hyper$Theta1" or
> "result$marginals.hyperpar$Theta1" for example.
>
> I calculate the mean, which is differ form the Theta1 shown in
> summary(result)

This is a different issue.  A likely explanation is how the mean is
calculated within the inla call itself.  Håvard may perhaps provide an
explanation for that; from my understanding, both the hyperpar "mean"
and "marginals.hyperpar" are generated from the internal
representation, which is _not_ in the form a discretised probability
density, so the discretised marginal shouldn't be expected to give the
same numeric answer for the mean as the internal calculations.

On Mon, 2012-10-01 at 14:45 -0700, Tim Keitt wrote:
> I wonder if someone could give an example of fitting a model with a
> known correlation matrix. I tried something like
>
>
> inla.fit1 = inla(y ~ x + f(i, model = "generic0", Cmatrix = cmat),
> family = "binomial", data = the_data)
>
>
>
> but then realized I don't really understand what I should give as
> cmat. The docs suggest that cmat might be a 0-1 structure matrix
> identifying rows that are related. I have a known correlation
> (kinship) matrix for the random effects. Can inla model that? How
> would I specify the model?

'cmat' is the precision matrix up to a scaling, so the precision matrix
for the generic0 model is

	prec * cmat

where prec is a scalar,

so if you have a known and fixed covariance matrx, then set

	cmat = solve(cov.mat)

and prec = 1,

f(i, ..., hyper = list(prec = list(initial = 0, fixed=TRUE)))

since the internal representation of a precision is in log scale, then

log(prec) = log(1) = 0

is the correct initial value.

On Thu, 2012-10-04 at 03:52 -0700, tim wrote:
> How does inla package select knots? I would like to do a smoothing

> knots or the number of knots needed?
>

the key argument is 'values', which by default is equal to the (sorted
and uniq'ed) covariates, but it does not have to be. also, the
locations of the knots for the RW models is not that critical, as long
as there are 'enough', as the model adjusting for that in a consistent
way.

Here is a small example showing this:

n = 100
## observation locations
x = runif(n,  min = 0,  max = n)
## extra knots
xx = 1:n

y = sin(x/10) + rnorm(n, sd = 0.001)
## these are 'knots' in the model
values = sort(c(x, xx))
formula = y ~ 1 + f(x, model="rw2",  values = values)
r = inla(formula,  data = list(y=y, x=x, values=values))
plot(r$summary.random$x$ID, r$summary.random$x$mean)

there are two ways out (if you really need it).

1. you have to do it yourself using the 'A'-matrix; see the FAQ. you
must write the spline as \sum b_k(x) w_k, for weights w_k and basis
functions b_k, and then make the linear predictor {w_k} and then create

immediately, but I can recreate one, if you really needs it...

2. if you just want to reduce the number of nots, then you can use

	f(inla.group(x), model="rw2")

 say, where inla.group(x), reduce the number of different values in 'x'
and group them around typical values, like

 [1] 2.0 2.0 2.0 5.5 5.5 5.5 5.5 9.0 9.0 9.0

and this will reduce the dimension of the model, without to much loss.
there is an argument 'n' in inla.group to control the number of groups.

let us know if this does not solve your problem.

(if you use RW models then dimension 85 is not large, so maybe you can
just use all? )

messages.body_plain:
Hi,

Can anyone help with a question I have relating to using INLA to fit joint longitudinal and time-to-event models as described in Guo and Carlin (2004)? The case study on this website and corresponding code is very helpful. However, I notice that Models X and XII are not currently implemented in the code. These are of the following type:

Continuous outcome linear predictor
eta[i]  = a[i] + b[i]*t[i]

where (a[i], b[i]) are the random-effects (latent fields) from a bivariate Gaussian model, and t[i] is a covariate (time).

Time-to-event outcome linear predictor
eta[i] = gamma* (a[i]+b[i]*t[i])

where gamma is an unknown fixed-effect (scaling parameter). Is there any way of currently using INLA's syntax to specify such a model?

A similar model where the linear predictor for the time-to-event outcome is
eta[i] = gamma1*a[i] + gamma[2]*b[i]
can be specified using the copy feature for each of a[i] and b[i] and specifying "fixed=FALSE" to estimate new scales. However, I can't see how to do this for a linear combination of the random-effects.

Help appreciated

Thanks
Mike

Thanks for your email. We added these examples quite some time ago and
it might be we can do the missing models X and XII now:

> Continuous outcome linear predictor
> eta[i]  = a[i] + b[i]*t[i]
>
> where (a[i], b[i]) are the random-effects (latent fields) from a
> bivariate Gaussian model, and t[i] is a covariate (time).

yes, this is in the model 'iid2d', just do inla.doc('iid2d'). a second
argument is the weight, so

	f(idx, weight, model='iid2d')

will add

	weight[i] * x[i]

to the linear predictor.   then you use 'copy' to duplicate it to get
the b*t, so

	f(i, model='iid2d', n = 2*n) + f(j, time, copy='i')

hmm, you might want to define 'n' in the first one, to set the
dimension. so if you have n bivariate (a,b), then n is 2*n. also  'j = i
+ n'

> Time-to-event outcome linear predictor
> eta[i] = gamma* (a[i]+b[i]*t[i])
>
> where gamma is an unknown fixed-effect (scaling parameter). Is there
> any way of currently using INLA's syntax to specify such a model?

yes, its getting tricky. you need several copies

f(i, model='iid2d', n=2*n) + f(j, copy='i', fixed=FALSE) + f(k, time,
copy='i', sameas='j', fixed=FALSE)

here 'i' is just NA's as you dont need them really,
the 'sameas' says that the random scaling the is 'same as' for model
'j'.

> A similar model where the linear predictor for the time-to-event
> outcome is
> eta[i] = gamma1*a[i] + gamma[2]*b[i]
> can be specified using the copy feature for each of a[i] and b[i] and
> specifying "fixed=FALSE" to estimate new scales. However, I can't see
> how to do this for a linear combination of the random-effects.

this is as the last example, except you do not need 'sameas', as then
you will get two different scalings.

TIPS: make a small simeple example with Gaussian response with a fixed
high precision and check that you'll get it right.

Here is a small example I tested against, at some point:

n = 10
y = c(1:n, 1:n, 2*(1:n))

x = c(1:n, rep(NA, 2*n))
xx = c(rep(NA,n), 1:n, rep(NA, n))
xxx = c(rep(NA, 2*n), 1:n)
www = c(rep(NA,2*n),rep(2,n))

formula = y ~ f(x) + f(xx, copy="x", fixed=FALSE) + f(xxx, www,
copy="x", same.as <http://same.as> = "xx")
r = inla(formula, data = data.frame(y,x,xx,xxx),verbose=TRUE,
        control.predictor =list(compute=TRUE),
        control.family = list(initial=4,fixed=T))

Let us know if you don't get it right ;-)

 logit(Disease probability) = Intercept + number of B alleles * log OR(B) + number of C alleles * log OR(C) + ....

Disease    Ntrials   A      B    C   D ....
yes           3          1       1    0    0                      for  AB genotype  (== BA genotype!!!)
no            2           2       0    0    0                     for AA genotype
yes           2          0       1    1    0                     for BC genotype

The more complicated idea is to include phylogenetic information, i.e. a tree of genetic distances between  different alleles.

Best regards,
Andreas

Hi

as Ryan suggested, there is a undocumented model called 'z'. this has
been around for quite a long time, but its internal implementation is
based on a 'hack' (and is hard to maintain) and therefore I want to
remove it and replace it with something more appropriate. morover, the
'z' model do

linear.predictor = ..... + Z %*% z

where z ~ N(0, prec * I), and Z is a fixed matrix, and the prior for
(log)prec is hyper=list(prec = list(prior=..,param=...)))

the model is internally expanded into 'm' submodels, so you'll get
results like this

r$summary.random$idx.1$mean

for the first element of 'z', and .2 for the second etc.

looking at the joint distribution for

	(Z %*% z, z)

we can rewrite this as a 'generic' model. this is the idea in some new
code, which is a wrapper to existing models,

new.z.model = inla.model.wrapper(covariates = Z,  model="joint",
Q = diag(m))

r = inla(y ~ 1 + f(idx,  model=new.z.model),
        data = list(y=y, idx=idx))

and then you'll get the posterior for (Z %*% z, z), so what you're after
is here:

r$summary.random$idx[(n+1):(n+m),"mean"]

as the last 'm' elements of that vector.  this model is more general as
'z' can have any prior precision matrix. the prior for its scaling, can
be set with hyper = list(prec = list(...))) as before

it might be we can do the 'wrapper'-call internally in the f-function,
so it will be hided from the user

to conclude: there is an approach on its way out, and a new better one
on its way in, but neither ones are stable. the new one is 'in progress'
and needs more work. I'll put this on the todo-list.

OOPS: in the future then model 'z' will go away and the new 'wrapper'
one will be changed (or even appear as something else, as we're not
convinced about the general usefulness of the 'wrapper'-based models),
but I'll post it here when its done.

*******************

EXAMPLE:

z = rnorm(m)
Z = matrix(rnorm(m*n), n, m)
y = 1 + Z %*% z
idx = 1:n

r = inla(y ~ 1 + f(idx,  model='z',  Z = Z),
        data = list(y=y, idx=idx, Z=Z))

new.z.model = inla.model.wrapper(covariates = Z,  model="joint", Q =
diag(m))
r = inla(y ~ 1 + f(idx,  model=new.z.model),
        data = list(y=y, idx=idx))

new.z.model = inla.model.wrapper(covariates = Z,  model="joint", Q =
diag(m))
r = inla(y ~ 1 + f(idx,  model=new.z.model),
        data = list(y=y, idx=idx))

print(r$summary.random$idx[(n+1):(n+m),"mean"] - z)

******************************
